lessons.title: Greetings and ¿Cómo estás?
lessons.objective: Greet a coworker at the right time of day and write '¿Cómo estás?' correctly.
lessons.hook: Every call with your Lima team starts with a greeting, so it should sound right.
lessons.aside: Peruvians often shorten 'buenos días' to 'buen día' in casual speech.
lessons.explain: Hola means hello and works at any time of day. Buenos días is used in the morning, buenas tardes in the afternoon, buenas noches in the evening and at night. ¿Cómo estás? means 'How are you?' to one person you treat informally. Spanish questions open with ¿ and close with ?. Accents matter: without accents, como means 'I eat' or 'like' and estas means 'these'. Example: at 3 p.m. on a call with your Lima team, say 'Hola, buenas tardes. ¿Cómo estás?'

Buenos días is used in the morning, buenas tardes in the afternoon, buenas noches in the evening and at night.

lessons.title: Spanish Sounds: Vowels, Silent h, ñ, Accents
lessons.objective: Pronounce and spell basic Spanish words, including the letter ñ.
lessons.hook: Clear sounds make your Peruvian coworkers understand you on the first try.
lessons.explain: Spanish has five vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u, each said short and pure, never glided like English 'day'. The letter h is silent: hola sounds like 'ola'. Ñ is a separate letter, said like 'ny' in canyon, the same sound as Hindi ञ; write it every time. A written accent marks the stressed syllable: estás is stressed on -tás. Example: mañana is said ma-NYA-na, with three pure 'a' sounds.

lessons.title: Me llamo: Saying Your Name
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself and ask someone's name without mixing up me and mi.
lessons.hook: Your name is the first thing new coworkers learn about you.
lessons.explain: Me llamo Alex means 'My name is Alex' (literally 'I call myself Alex'). Me means 'myself'; mi means 'my'. So 'mi llamo' is wrong; the correct form is 'me llamo'. lessons.title: Tú and Usted: Informal and Formal 'You'
lessons.objective: Choose tú or usted with Peruvian coworkers and clients, and use the matching verb form.
lessons.hook: Using the wrong 'you' with a client can sound rude or oddly stiff.
lessons.explain: Spanish has two words for 'you'. Tú is informal 'you'; usted is formal 'you'. Usted takes the same verb form as él/ella: ¿Cómo está usted? not ¿Cómo estás usted? With usted, 'What is your name?' becomes ¿Cómo se llama usted? In Peru, usted is common with clients, managers and people you've just met; switch to tú when a coworker uses it with you. This works much like Hindi तुम versus आप. Example: to the client's director, 'Buenos días, ¿cómo está usted?'

lessons.title: Ser: Soy, Eres, Es
lessons.objective: Say who you are, what you do and where you're from.
lessons.hook: After your name, coworkers will ask what you do and where you're from.
lessons.explain: Use ser for who you are. Soy means 'I am' for identity, job or origin. Eres means 'you are' (tú); es means 'he/she is' or 'you are' (usted). Spanish usually drops yo because soy already shows the subject. Job nouns take no article: Soy ingeniero, not Soy un ingeniero. Soy de la India means 'I am from India'. Example: 'Hola, me llamo Alex. Soy de la India. Soy desarrollador.'

lessons.title: Present Tense -ar Verbs: Trabajo en...
lessons.objective: Conjugate regular -ar verbs and say where you work.
lessons.hook: 'I work at...' is the most useful sentence for your job, with no English words mixed in.
lessons.explain: Regular -ar verbs drop -ar and add endings: -o (yo), -as (tú), -a (él/ella/usted), -amos (nosotros), -an (ellos/ustedes). Trabajar means 'to work'; trabajo means 'I work'. Trabajo en [place] means 'I work at...', as in Trabajo en Lima. The same word as a noun gives mi trabajo, meaning 'my job': Mi trabajo es interesante. Example: hablar becomes hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, hablan.

lessons.title: Hoy, Mañana, Ayer

lessons.title: Saying No: No + Verb, and Sí
lessons.objective: Make negative sentences and answer yes/no questions.
lessons.hook: 'I'm not working tomorrow' is just as important as 'I am'.
lessons.explain: Put no directly before the verb to make it negative. No trabajo hoy means 'I don't work today'. Spanish needs no helper like English 'do': no + verb is enough.
